title: Zdravo, Sarajevo!
reviewerNotes: Exemplar chapter — ready for human review before publish.
storyBeat: Ana lands in Sarajevo and takes her first walk through Baščaršija, practicing greetings and new letter sounds.

vocabulary: Basic greetings (zdravo, dobar dan, hvala, molim)
Letters with diacritics: č, ć, š, ž, đ, dž
grammar: Simple greeting exchanges (no full conjugation yet)

Warm everyday greetings in Bosnia and Herzegovina

grammar.title: The Latin Bosnian alphabet
grammar.explanation: Bosnian is written with the Latin alphabet in this book. Most letters sound familiar. Six special letters matter a lot: č, ć, š, ž, đ, and the digraph dž. We never use Cyrillic here.

examples.english: jar (ć is softer, closer to 't' + soft 'ch')

grammar.title: Greeting exchanges
grammar.explanation: Start simple. Say a greeting, hear one back, then add hvala or molim. Formal day greetings use dobar dan; friends often say zdravo.

culture.title: Baščaršija — Sarajevo’s old heart
culture.body: Baščaršija is the historic bazaar of Sarajevo: narrow streets, copper shops, cafés, and the sound of footsteps on stone. Ana arrives with a backpack and a phrase list. Shopkeepers greet visitors with a warm Dobar dan! Learning greetings here is not just polite — it opens doors (and often a free smile). The special letters in Baščaršija (š, č) are your first real Bosnian workout.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A — Letters that look new
lessonBlocks.body: Look at these six: č ć š ž đ dž. Pair each with a word you can feel in your mouth. Čaj (tea). Ćup (jar). Šuma (forest). Žena (woman). Đak (pupil). Džezva (the little pot for Bosnian coffee). Say them slowly. Ana practices on the plane: čaj, čaj, čaj — then walks into Baščaršija and sees a real džezva in a shop window.
tips: č vs ć: č is harder; ć is softer and shorter
dž is one sound, like English j in jam
Read street signs out loud — Sarajevo is full of practice

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B — Your first greetings
lessonBlocks.body: Memorize this mini set: Zdravo (hi), Dobar dan (good day), Dobro jutro (good morning), Dobra večer (good evening), Hvala (thanks), Molim (please / you're welcome), Doviđenja (goodbye), Da / Ne (yes / no). Use Dobar dan with people you do not know well. Use Zdravo with friends — or with Emir, once you meet him tomorrow.
tips: Smile helps more than perfect pronunciation
If you forget, Hvala still works almost everywhere

funFacts.title: Baščaršija means ‘main market’
funFacts.body: The name comes from Turkish roots meaning the chief marketplace. Today it is still full of craft shops and cafés.

funFacts.title: One letter, one sound
funFacts.body: Bosnian spelling is mostly phonetic: what you see is what you say. That helps beginners a lot once the special letters click.

funFacts.title: Cats of the čaršija
funFacts.body: Sarajevo’s old town is famous for friendly street cats. Mrvica is fictional — but her attitude is very local.

questions.question: What does 'zdravo' mean?
questions.explanation: Zdravo is the friendly everyday hello.

questions.question: Which greeting is more polite with strangers during the day?
questions.explanation: Dobar dan is the polite daytime greeting.

questions.question: Which word means 'thank you'?
questions.explanation: Hvala = thank you. Molim can mean please or you're welcome.

questions.question: The letter š sounds most like English…
questions.explanation: Š is like sh in ship — as in Baščaršija.

questions.question: A džezva is…
questions.explanation: Džezva is the little pot used for Bosnian coffee.

questions.question: Baščaršija is…
questions.explanation: Baščaršija is the historic market heart of Sarajevo.

questions.question: Which pair shows a harder vs softer 'ch'-like sound?
options: dž vs đ only as vowels
questions.explanation: Č is harder; ć is softer — a classic beginner pair.
